content: Childhood-onset schizophrenia is defined as schizophrenia that begins before the age of 13. Although it is a rare condition, individuals who develop schizophrenia at such an early age often experience a more severe form of the illness, which is associated with a poor long-term prognosis. Antipsychotic medications are one of the primary treatment options for managing this serious mental health condition. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of antipsychotic medications in children diagnosed with childhood-onset schizophrenia. To achieve this, researchers conducted a systematic search of the Cochrane Schizophrenia Group Trials Register in November 2006 and February 2007. They also reviewed references from identified studies and contacted pharmaceutical companies and trial authors to gather additional information. The study included randomized clinical trials involving children and adolescents diagnosed with schizophrenia before the age of 13. These trials compared the effects of one antipsychotic drug with another or with a placebo. Data from the trials were carefully selected, assessed for quality, and extracted. Trials were excluded if more than 50% of participants in any group were lost to follow-up. For dichotomous data, relative risk (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated using random effects models, and the number needed to treat (NNT) was determined when appropriate. For continuous data, the weighted mean difference (WMD) was calculated. Out of 2,062 citations, six relevant trials were identified. These trials were categorized into three types of comparisons: atypical antipsychotics versus typical antipsychotics, atypical antipsychotics versus other atypical antipsychotics, and typical antipsychotics versus other typical antipsychotics. The only comparison that showed significant differences between treatment groups was atypical antipsychotics versus typical antipsychotics. One study demonstrated that the atypical antipsychotic clozapine was more effective than the typical antipsychotic haloperidol in treating treatment-resistant childhood-onset schizophrenia. Specifically, clozapine showed greater improvement on the Children's Global Assessment Scale (CGAS) (n=21, WMD 17.00, CI 7.74 to 26.26) and the Bunney-Hamburg Psychosis Rating Scale (n=21, WMD -3.60, CI -6.64 to -0.56). However, clozapine was associated with a significantly higher risk of adverse effects. Participants taking clozapine were three times more likely to experience drowsiness (1 RCT, n=21, RR 3.30, CI 1.23 to 8.85, NNH 2, CI 2 to 17). Additionally, half of the children receiving clozapine developed neutropenia, a potentially serious condition characterized by a low level of neutrophils (1 RCT, n=21, RR 12, CI 0.75 to 192.86). The authors concluded that there is currently limited evidence regarding the effects of antipsychotic medications for childhood-onset schizophrenia due to the small number of relevant trials. While clozapine showed some benefits compared to haloperidol, these benefits were counterbalanced by an increased risk of serious side effects. Larger and more rigorous clinical trials are needed to provide conclusive evidence on the efficacy and safety of antipsychotic medications for this population.
